figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Overview of SkillOpt. The target model executes tasks with a current skill, an additional frontier optimizer model converts trajectories into bounded add/delete/replace skill edits, and a held-out gate accepts only edits that improve validation performance. Accepted edits are exported as a reusable skill artifact, while rejected edits become negative feedback for later updates.
figures.headline: Bounded edits from an optimizer model are accepted only through a held-out gate, and rejected edits feed later updates.
citing_sentences: Figure 1 gives a schematic view of this loop.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Pipeline of SkillOpt. A frozen target model executes a rollout batch with the current skill; an optimizer model performs minibatch reflection over successes and failures, proposes bounded add/delete/replace edits, merges and ranks them under a scheduled edit budget, and accepts the candidate skill only through a held-out validation gate. Across epochs, the slow/meta update retains longer-horizon lessons without changing the target model.
figures.headline: The pipeline combines rollouts, minibatch reflection, bounded edits, and a held-out gate, with a slow update across epochs.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Performance trends across epoch checkpoints on three benchmarks: (a) SpreadsheetBench, (b) SearchQA, and (c) LiveMath. For each checkpoint, we report the training rollout score, the selection-best score on the validation set, and the final performance on the unseen test set. The results show how skill quality evolves during optimization and whether the checkpoint preferred by validation selection aligns with the checkpoint that yields the best generalization to the test set.
figures.headline: Validation-selected epoch checkpoints tend to track held-out test scores on SpreadsheetBench, SearchQA, and LiveMath.
citing_sentences: Table 2, Figure 3, and Table 3 test the design choices in the optimizer using GPT–5.5 as both the target and the optimizer.

Figure 3 complements these numerical ablations: validation checkpoints track held-out test performance across epochs, confirming that the gate tends to select skills that generalize rather than skills that only fit the selection split.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Representative learned rules, one per benchmark, extracted from the final best_skill.md of the GPT–5.5 / GPT–5.5 runs in Table 6. Each rule is verbatim from the deployed skill. Notably, every rule is procedural rather than instance-specific, and several encode forms of discipline (answer formatting, evidence binding, search-frontier management) that frontier models do not apply zero-shot.
figures.headline: Each benchmark's representative learned rule is procedural and names no specific question, file, or entity.
citing_sentences: Figure 4 reproduces one representative learned rule per benchmark, taken verbatim from the final best_skill.md of each case study in Table 6.

abstract: Agent skills today are hand-crafted, generated one-shot, or evolved through loosely controlled self-revision, none of which behaves like a deep-learning optimizer for the skill, and none of which reliably improves over its starting point under feedback. We argue the skill should instead be trained as the external state of a frozen agent, with the same discipline that makes weight-space optimization reproducible. SkillOpt is, to our knowledge, the first systematic controllable text-space optimizer for agent skills: a separate optimizer model turns scored rollouts into bounded add/delete/replace edits on a single skill document, and an edit is accepted only when it strictly improves a held-out validation score. A textual learning-rate budget, rejected-edit buffer, and epoch-wise slow/meta update make skill training stable while adding zero inference-time model calls at deployment. Across six benchmarks, seven target models, and three execution harnesses (direct chat, Codex, Claude Code), SkillOpt is best or tied on all 52 evaluated (model, benchmark, harness) cells and beats every per-cell competitor among human, one-shot LLM, Trace2Skill, TextGrad, GEPA, and EvoSkill skills. On GPT-5.5 it lifts the average no-skill accuracy by +23.5 points in direct chat, by +24.8 inside the Codex agentic loop, and by +19.1 inside Claude Code. Transfer experiments further show that optimized skill artifacts retain value when moved across model scales, between Codex and Claude Code execution environments, and to a nearby math benchmark without further optimization. Code: https://aka.ms/skillopt

sections.body: The paper treats the skill document as trainable state for a frozen agent. A separate optimizer model reads scored rollouts and proposes add, delete, or replace edits. A textual learning-rate budget caps the edits applied per step, and a candidate is kept only if it strictly improves a held-out selection score. The deployed output is a single compact `best_skill.md` file. On GPT–5.5 in direct chat, the average gain over no skill across six benchmarks is +23.5 points.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: SkillOpt optimizes an agent's skill document as external state, with validation-gated edits and no weight updates.

sections.body: GEPA, ABSTRAL, and EvoTest optimize prompts, multi-agent designs, or test-time system configurations, but not a persistent reusable skill. Other systems construct or refine skills from lifelong experience, trajectory lessons, failure analysis, or reinforcement learning, with emphasis on discovery, sharing, and evolutionary search. The paper states a narrower problem: training one compact domain skill with trajectory batches, reflection minibatches, textual learning rates, validation gates, rejected-edit buffers, and slow/meta updates. The output is an auditable `best_skill.md` produced without changing model weights.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior skill work mainly builds or evolves skill libraries, while prompt optimizers target prompts rather than a persistent skill.

sections.body: Each step runs a rollout batch of the frozen target model on training tasks and records messages, tool calls, verifier feedback, and outputs. An optimizer model reflects on failure and success minibatches separately, then merges the proposals hierarchically, giving priority to failure corrections. A bounded edit budget $L_t$ caps how many edits are applied. Patch mode allows append, insert, replace, and delete, and step edits cannot change the protected slow-update section. The candidate is evaluated on the selection split and accepted only if it strictly improves the current selection score. Rejected edits and their score drops go into an epoch-local buffer used by later reflection calls.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Each step edits the skill with bounded add, delete and replace operations, accepted only if held-out selection score strictly improves.

sections.body: Experiments cover six benchmarks, seven target models from GPT to Qwen, and three harnesses: direct chat, Codex, and Claude Code. SkillOpt is best or tied on all 52 evaluated (model, benchmark, harness) cells, compared with no-skill, human, one-shot LLM, Trace2Skill, TextGrad, GEPA, and EvoSkill baselines. On GPT–5.5 in direct chat, it beats the best per-cell baseline by +5.4 points on average. Over no skill, GPT–5.5 gains +24.8 in Codex and +19.1 in Claude Code. All scores are on disjoint held-out test splits. ALFWorld is omitted under the two harnesses because it needs persistent embodied interaction.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: SkillOpt is best or tied on all 52 evaluated cells, lifting GPT–5.5 by 23.5 points in direct chat.

sections.body: The conclusion is that SkillOpt turns skill improvement into a controlled learning process rather than ad hoc prompt revision. Across six benchmarks, seven models, and three execution modes, it is best or tied-best on 52 of 52 cells. The per-benchmark case studies attribute the gains to compact artifacts assembled from only 1–4 accepted edits. The authors report that the skills transfer across model scales, harnesses, and nearby benchmarks. Named future directions include skill libraries, reward-free validation for open-ended tasks, and self-distillation into the target model.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Compact skills optimized this way transfer across model scales, harnesses and a nearby benchmark without weight updates.

sections.body: The appendix gives the executable details of the method and the prompt contracts for failure analysis, success analysis, merging, ranking, slow update, and the optimizer meta skill. Appendix B lists limitations: the loop needs scored trajectories or reliable feedback, training adds rollout and optimizer cost, and a single skill may not suit heterogeneous domains. It also notes that transferred skills need careful held-out evaluation. Appendix C gives the protocol: native evaluators, a default 2:1:7 split, four epochs with rollout batch size 40, and patch operations `append`, `insert_after`, `replace`, and `delete`.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix lists the optimizer prompt contracts, limitations, and experimental protocol with patch and split details.
